A1.justification: Both PDFs describe CANDI and contain readable main text, equations, figures, algorithms, references, and appendices. Their substantial reformatting and section moves do not prevent reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original Text8 and OpenWebText generation experiments, QM9 guidance experiments, corruption simulations, and inference analyses, including Figures 6–14.

after.justification: v3 retains these empirical results and adds simulations comparing corruption of learned GPT-2 embeddings and random embeddings in Appendix B.5 and Figure 10.

M1.justification: The hybrid masking/Gaussian kernel, weighted cross-entropy objective, corruption bias, preconditioning, exact and approximate inference, and classifier guidance are retained. Equation and pseudocode corrections align with the previously described procedure; the newly specified bias weight is additional implementation disclosure.

E1.justification: Appendix B.5 adds a fixed-embedding corruption scenario using pretrained GPT-2 embeddings and matched random embedding populations. This extends the earlier one-hot simulations and generation experiments, while Text8, OpenWebText, and QM9 coverage remains unchanged.

E2.justification: Corresponding comparisons retain the same participants: MDLM and continuous one-hot/embedding models for vocabulary scaling; MDLM, DUO, and AR for OWT; and MDLM/UDLM for QM9. The new random-versus-learned embedding simulation does not add a generative baseline evaluated against CANDI.

E3.justification: The new embedding simulation introduces vocabulary/noise sweeps and isotropic Gaussian controls fitted to learned embeddings' mean and variance. Existing generation temperature and NFE settings are retained. v3 also removes v1's main-text 50k-step anchoring statement; the PDFs do not establish that the existing experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: Appendix B.5 adds a targeted check of whether learned embeddings exhibit the corruption behavior predicted using comparison independence, including vocabulary-subset repetitions. Earlier temperature analyses, higher-NFE results, and exact-versus-approximate inference comparisons remain.

E5.justification: The new simulation reports 1,000 trials per vocabulary/noise condition and five random vocabulary subsets, except for the full vocabulary. Figure 10 introduces shaded bands without defining their statistical meaning. This does not establish additional training-seed repetitions or new uncertainty estimates for the retained generation results.

E6.justification: New Figure 10 reports similar corruption curves for learned GPT-2 and matched random embeddings, with vocabulary-sensitive discrete corruption and comparatively stable continuous degradation. Existing benchmark plots, throughput results, inference comparisons, and generated-sample metrics are retained without numerical changes; v3 Figure 11 repeats the existing temperature comparison.

T1.justification: v3 Appendix B.4 replaces v1 Appendix A.4's embedding-corruption factorization argument with comparison-event definitions and an explicit independence assumption. This materially changes the stated conditions supporting the embedding generalization, although its final scaling expression is retained. Appendix C.1 also corrects mask-conditioning cases and adds mask-state delta factors to the joint reverse transition.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same central contributions: token identifiability, temporal dissonance, hybrid corruption that addresses it, improved low-NFE generation, and guidance using ordinary classifiers. Condensation and additional supporting material do not redefine these claims.

C2.justification: New Appendix B.6 distinguishes contextual latent diffusion from tokenwise embedding diffusion, explaining why contextual decoding can avoid the proposed failure mechanism and interpreting encoder/decoder pretraining as separately learning discrete structure. Appendix B.5 additionally interprets its simulations as support for comparison independence. Existing benchmark interpretations and higher-NFE qualifications remain.

D1.justification: v3 adds a project-page code pointer, specifies the corruption-bias weight as lambda = 0.5, and explains Text8 word processing and validity: lowercase, whitespace-delimited words appearing in training or test data. It also documents the new embedding simulation. Most architecture, hardware, training-time, and sampling information was already present.

R1.justification: v3 adds latent-diffusion positioning through Lovelace et al., Meshchaninov et al., and Shabalin et al., plus citations to Ou et al. and Pynadath et al. (2026). It removes the gradient-based discrete-MCMC paragraph and its associated citations. The CADD/CCDD comparison is retained in Appendix A rather than newly introduced.

P1.justification: The main narrative is substantially condensed and reorganized. Concurrent works moves to Appendix A; detailed inference, guidance, training-objective, and frontier-evaluation explanations move into expanded appendices. Sampling-trick and architectural explanations are rewritten, alongside new appendix subsections and conference front matter.

P2.justification: The single-column main text becomes a two-column conference layout, substantially changing figure sizing, placement, captions, and text flow. v3 adds the eight-panel embedding simulation as Figure 10 and redisplays Figure 5 as Figure 11. Existing plots are retained and redistributed, with appendix figures renumbered.

improvement.justification: v3 improves transparency through an explicit embedding-independence assumption, a targeted supporting simulation, clearer applicability discussion, and useful reproduction details such as the bias weight and Text8 validity rules. These are limited gains: the main benchmark evidence is unchanged, and similar learned/random embedding corruption curves do not by themselves establish comparison independence or fully resolve the embedding argument.
